title: Application Architecture: Web, Workers, and Services
summary: Split the system into layers that can grow, deploy, and fail independently.
keyPoints: Separate the edge, application, worker, and data layers so each can scale and fail independently.
Stateless application instances are easy to scale, replace, and deploy.
A modular monolith is a valid default; microservices trade operational simplicity for independent ownership.
Service discovery maps names to healthy instances, and health checks decide what is in rotation.
Every synchronous call needs a deadline, and every retried write needs idempotency.

complexity.note: Can fail independently of local code.
Keep business logic out of the gateway.
Good for slow work, not for the response the user waits on.

commonMistakes: Adopting microservices without a concrete scaling, ownership, or release constraint.
Calling services independently but sharing one database schema, which preserves hidden coupling.
Putting business rules in the API gateway or load balancer.
Adding retries to every call without a deadline, a limit, or an idempotency key.
interviewNotes: Name the layers and what each one owns before naming technologies.
Say what is stateful; that is what makes scaling hard.
Justify a monolith or microservices from constraints, not fashion.
Describe the timeout, retry, and idempotency behavior at every network boundary.

checkYourself.question: Why is a stateless application tier easier to scale?
checkYourself.answer: Any instance can serve any request, so traffic can be spread freely and a failed instance can be replaced without losing user state.

checkYourself.question: What is a modular monolith?
checkYourself.answer: One deployable application with clear internal module boundaries and interfaces. It keeps deployment simple while reducing the cost of future extraction.

checkYourself.question: What should a service discovery health check verify?
checkYourself.answer: Enough to tell whether the instance can serve traffic, without depending on every shared dependency. A check that fails for a shared outage can remove every healthy instance at once.
